scope: Single-reviewer position character and newly opened rook file. Reviewed from legal root candidates and independent reply frames, before opening classifier results. Uncertain axes receive null.

cases.rationale: White develops on the already open d-file and has several king-safety move orders.
The competing a- and c-pawns and rook activity differ. The endgame lines leave exact tactical significance uncertain.
Several viable moves contest the e-file after the central exchange. The f8 rook has no repeated newly opened file entry.
Na4 attacks the queen and changes the double rook exchange. Its large gain comes immediately.
Both sides must deal with the e-pawn plus the fixed queenside pawns and blockading pieces. Short checks alone are inconclusive.
King centralisation and cutting the king off with rook checks explain the endgame plans.
An already open d-file and control of c4 persist across different knight placements. The severity of lesser tactical differences is unclear.
Nxe5 is the only searched move near equality. The other choices let the bishop capture on c6 under concrete pressure.
Nb2+ changes the a-pawn outcome. The remaining knight and opposed passed pawns still dictate separate plans after the capture.
Different preparations all contest c4 and the c-file. The equal captures leave viable strategic choices.
White can advance the a-pawn or increase rook pressure while Black keeps the g-pawn on the rook file.
Rxd2 is exact after Bxd4. On Bxd4 and Nfxd4 the removal of the d-pawn opens a lasting route for Black's rook to d8 and pressure on d2.
White can change the central tension or start kingside play. A secondary h4 line opens the h-file but another competitive route is uncertain.
Rook activity on the second rank and the knight's route through e5 recur in the balanced alternatives.
axb4 attacks the knight and avoids losing the c3 knight. White's a-file and Black's remaining outposts shape the subsequent play. The other root choices have poor evaluations.
cxd4 takes the bishop and avoids Qxe5. The second plausible-looking root only gives a tactical queen exchange.
The two d4 captures leave different central pawns and give the rooks different files. There is no repeated opening of the same rook file.
The choice is about rook activity, pawn advances and defending the a- and b-pawns with several viable move orders.
Keeping c6 available and fixing the central pawns changes the file and bishop play. No common newly opened rook file is observed.
The a-pawn advance and rook placement on the a-file constrain White's defence through all credible lines.
Nb3 avoids the attack on the d2 knight. The still-active queens can trade into a distinct structure with the f-pawn on e3.
Several choices contest the already open d-file or use the c-file for coordination. Black can support d5 after the bishop capture.
The rook and queen force a short mate. There is no stable strategic phase in the leading line.
The handling of g-file pressure differs after the bishop takes on f4. Black's rook can use an existing pawnless g-file.
The black d-pawn is advanced and exchanged in both rook choices. It leaves Black with a continuing d-file rook presence and a capture on d4 in the corroborated second route.
Whether the a3-pawn is taken immediately or after a2 changes the later rook activity. White already has no a-pawn in these lines.
Both sides use a file that was already open, and d4 changes the central fight in the alternative plans.
Choosing which piece takes d6 changes the black h-pawn's immediate capture and leaves different pawn structures. Rooks contest an already available c-file.
Several queen moves permit the e5 break, king safety and e-file activity. The en passant capture does not establish a second tactical purpose.
Rxa5 immediately wins a rook through the undefended double capture and stays decisively ahead.
Bc4 targets the bishop on d3 and induces a concrete minor-piece concession. No comparable positional purpose is shown.
Ne6 threatens a fork around f8, with a pawn on e6 in several branches. Actual sustained rook-file use beyond the tactical exchanges is uncertain.
Black's advanced outside pawn persists across different knight moves. The shown captures and reroutes establish concrete promotion resources.
The rook trade requires the queen recapture. Otherwise White changes f- and h-pawn pressure while Black uses a different rook plan.
The serious choices use checks to win on h3 immediately. The h-file activity is part of the forced material gain.
Black's deeply advanced f-pawn limits White's pieces and has multiple concrete promotion continuations.
Clearing White's e-file gives a rook sustained access after both fxg4 and e6. The tactical branches contain immediate checks and captures on the seventh rank.
The early knight sacrifice and captures dominate the first exchanges. Independent long-term value after liquidation is uncertain.
Black can trade queens into a position with distinct bishop and central pawn roles or keep queens with similar scores.
White's f-break and queenside tension are resolved in different orders. No same newly opened file is actively used in two choices.
Immediate checks or knight moves prevent a forcing king attack. The black c-passer remains a separate winning resource.
Rooks contest an already open e-file and trade into c-file pressure. The significance of the short knight captures is uncertain.
Bxe5 prevents forcing pressure after Qh5. It also diverts the d-pawn to e5 and permits Black's lasting d4 advance.
The immediate capture and queen checks create threats around the exposed king. The e2-pawn remains a constraint in both near-best approaches.
Black improves minor pieces and uses opposing-colour king-side weaknesses. The timing of captures varies without one tested tactical dependency.
Qxh6 and other candidates prepare direct captures around the king. The material wins make independent strategic purpose unclear.
The bishop checks and pawn exchanges alter the tactical defence. White's f-file may open, but concrete use in a second line is inconclusive.
e4 accelerates a passed pawn and exact queen-fork or checking attacks arise when the white king is displaced.
Capturing on b5 limits the queenside passer. Other moves concede a durable structural problem, while the tactical explanation is unclear.
Taking d5 directly and first repositioning the bishop produce different concrete exchanges and keep the white rook active on d6 or d7. White already lacks a d-pawn.
The d-pawn has two different advancement or exchange plans. The second independent newly opened rook-file line is not established.
The Nxe5 resource exploits the central advance. Black also keeps the queenside pawn advantage and the bishop's diagonal.
Rexd2 preserves control of c3, while Rcxd2 lets the rook take there and changes the exchange. Several other choices keep the c-file pressure.
